expected_evidence: A continent-wide (or global) layer at ~12,900 cal BP (Younger Dryas Boundary) showing anomalous platinum-group element (Pt, Ir) spikes
Nanodiamonds, cubic/hexagonal diamond polymorphs, or lonsdaleite in the YDB sediment layer
Magnetic microspherules and carbon spherules consistent with high-temperature impact/airburst formation
A 'black mat' organic-rich sediment layer directly overlying the proposed impact horizon at multiple North American sites
Continent-scale biomass-burning markers: soot, charcoal peaks, and polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons synchronous with the YD onset
An identifiable impact crater or crater field (e.g., proposed candidates like the Hiawatha Glacier crater) datable to ~12,900 BP
Coincident megafaunal extinction horizon and abrupt decline/disappearance of Clovis-culture archaeological material directly above the layer
Independent replication of the above signatures at geographically dispersed sites with consistent, tightly-constrained dating
Ice-core or varve-based chronostratigraphic markers (e.g., ammonium, sulfate, or dust spikes) precisely dating an abrupt onset event at 10,950 BCE
Population genetic bottleneck signals in megafaunal or early human DNA dated to this interval
response.rationale: This hypothesis corresponds to the Younger Dryas Impact Hypothesis (YDIH), a real and actively contested position in Quaternary geology/archaeology (model-prior, not verified against supplied source text). If a cosmic impact or airburst triggered YD cooling, the primary expected evidence is geological (impact ejecta layers, PGE/iridium anomalies, nanodiamonds, microspherules, black mats, crater structures) and secondarily material/archaeological (megafaunal extinction and Clovis discontinuity) and astronomical/geochronological (precisely dated ice-core or varve markers). The detectability table assigns relatively high scores to geological (0.65) and astronomical (0.7) evidence for the younger-dryas period, and moderate scores to material (0.35) and genetic (0.3) evidence, reflecting that sedimentary and glacial-ice archives from ~13,000 years ago are well-preserved and routinely sampled -- this is not a deep-time detectability problem the way Paleozoic events are. Textual (0.0), linguistic (0.05), oral_tradition (0.1), and iconographic (0.1) evidence are essentially inapplicable since no writing or durable symbolic record exists this early. Given that geological/geochemical evidence of an impact of the claimed continental-to-global scale should plausibly survive and be detectable with modern methods (as demonstrated by successful, unambiguous impact-layer detection at the much older K-Pg boundary), a genuine low-detectability explanation for absence of confirmed evidence is only partially justified here. This is consistent with the actual scientific record (model-prior): despite extensive search, independent teams have largely failed to replicate the original platinum/nanodiamond findings, and no confirmed impact crater has been dated to this interval, which many researchers take as evidence against the hypothesis rather than merely a detection failure. The mechanism tag 'dating-uncertainty' in the hypothesis itself acknowledges this -- chronological imprecision across sites is a genuine complicating factor, but is a separate issue from whether the physical impact markers would have survived. I therefore suggest a detectability adjustment around 0.5, weighting the higher-detectability geological/astronomical evidence types (primary to this hypothesis) against the near-zero detectability of textual/linguistic/iconographic types that are irrelevant this deep in prehistory, while cautioning that low detectability should not be used to fully explain away the substantial negative/non-replicated evidence already reported in the literature for this specific claim.
